Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-19
Start: 15:12 UTC
Duration: 68 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE); Diego Martinez (Redwood SE); Priya Rao (Mistral, Head of ML); Tom Gallagher (Mistral, Infra); Sofia Kim (Mistral, PM)

Summary: See metadata summary above.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Avery: ok, good morning / afternoon everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick intro — i'm avery, i'm the account lead. diego will run the deep-dive on throughput and the kv handoff stuff. priya, thanks for organizing.
[00:12] Priya: yeah thanks avery. we wanted to really understand how redwood would scale for our interactive assistant workload — lots of short requests with heavy context reuse.
[00:22] Diego: perfect, that's exactly what we'll cover. two parts: 1) how continuous batching + concurrency impacts per-token cost and p95 latency; 2) session / kv handoff (we sometimes call it prefix reuse) to reduce compute. we'll also walk through a cost sim for your traffic mix.
[00:40] Tom: quick note, infra constraint — we have a private VPC option for pilot, and we need envelopes for KMS and TLS certs. so any configs must work with our HSM.
[00:51] Avery: noted. we'll include kms notes and the SOC2 snippet in the followup.
[00:57] Sofia: and success criteria — we care about p95 under 350ms for short queries and under 1.2s for multi-turn sessions; and unit cost below $0.00045 per token equivalent.
[01:12] Diego: ok cool, we'll map sim assumptions to those SLAs. before we dive, shared artifacts — we have a cost-sim sheet and a smallbench harness. link: https://redwood.app/sheets/sim-mistral-10-19 (we'll re-send).
[01:30] Diego: starting with batching: continuous batching groups in-flight tokens across requests to use GPU efficiently. pro: much lower per-token cost. con: introduces queueing delay that grows with target throughput and batch windows.
[01:47] Priya: i'm still fuzzy — at what concurrency does batching start hurting our p95? we have users doing 1–3 requests/sec each.
[01:56] Diego: good question. in our sim, for your token distribution (median 24 tokens, tail 180), batching helps once sustained concurrency >~10 per model replica. below that, smaller micro-batches win for latency. so there's a sweet spot.
[02:15] Sofia: what about prefetching / kv prewarm — can we pre-populate kv for the 20% of sessions that are expected to hit a known context?
[02:24] Diego: yes, that's the kv handoff pattern. we call it session affinity + prefix reuse. two approaches: synchronous prefetch on warm paths, or async backfill. prefetch trades write/read ops for reduced inference cost. one common gotcha: if prefetch is too broad you increase kv costs and network IO.
[02:46] Tom: is kv kept on the GPU host or in an external store? concerns about network hops.
[02:52] Diego: Redwood supports both local hot-kv (co-located, low latency memory) and an external KV (s3/redis style). for strict latency SLOs we recommend hot-kv co-located with the inference node; for long-tail cold store we push to remote. there's a hybrid mode where we attempt a local hit and fallback to remote.
[03:14] Priya: are there cases where caching actually increases cost?
[03:18] Diego: yes — over-aggressive caching or prefetch increases read/write ops and memory pressure. Example: if you prefetch entire session histories for every login, your hit rate drops and you pay both for extra kv ops and for larger batch overhead. the sim models this: hit rate vs prefetch width curve.
[03:36] [crosstalk] Priya: mm-hmm, that makes sense
[03:40] Diego: i'll show the sim now — opening slide 3: baseline — no cache, small-batch concurrency 8, p95 ~ 420ms, cost $0.0012 per request.
[03:52] Diego: scenario A — medium batching and hot-kv with 60% hit rate for prefixes: p95 drops to 310ms, cost per request ~ $0.00048. big drop.
[04:08] Sofia: that's impressive. what's the assumed kv op cost in the sim?
[04:13] Diego: we model kv read at $0.00001/op and write at $0.00002/op for external store; local hot-kv is amortized into host cost (we model as $0.000005/hit). these are conservative numbers.
[04:25] Priya: can you explain the handoff flow end-to-end? like from our app to redwood to model?
[04:31] Diego: sure. flow: app -> redwood proxy -> router selects replica based on session affinity -> check local kv for prefix; if hit, pre-append to prompt (shortened representation), if miss, call remote kv then append; inference executes with reduced autoregressive steps; if new tokens generated, optionally write back a compressed kv entry.
[04:56] Tom: who owns the compressed kv schema? we have to align on serialization.
[05:00] Avery: we usually provide a recommended serializer and have a small shim you can drop in. we'll share the serializer snippet in the followup.
[05:06] Priya: latency budget question — during fallbacks (local miss -> remote), do we have to pay a heavy latency penalty that breaks p95?
[05:14] Diego: fallback penalty exists but we mitigate with async prefetch. also router-level policies allow routing that request to a lower-latency replica in a different pool when miss probability is high. multi-tier fallbacks help avoid long tail spikes.
[05:30] Sofia: what's the operational overhead for us? like rehydration, eviction policies, monitoring?
[05:36] Diego: Redwood Console exposes eviction metrics, hit/miss heatmaps, and a suggested TTL policy. we can also provide automated suggestions (Optimize) for tuning prefetch width and TTL based on your workload trace.
[05:50] Priya: the Optimize product — will it automatically change runtime policies or just recommend?
[05:56] Diego: defaults are recommendations, but you can opt-in to automatic tuning in a pilot. for enterprise pilots we usually keep it manual until we validate the sim results.
[06:05] Avery: let's walk the sensitivity table in the sheet — diego can screen share the numbers.
[06:12] Diego: (screen) ok sheet visible. row 1: assumptions — token costs, batch efficiency curve, concurrency mix. row 6: hit rates 0–80%. row 9: cost per 1M requests. see column K — when hit rate >45% and concurrency >12, savings exceed 60% vs baseline.
[06:33] Priya: if we need to keep everything on-prem (private deployment), how much do the numbers change?
[06:39] Diego: on-prem removes egress and managed infra line items, but you absorb hardware amortization and ops. our sim has an on-prem toggle — cost per request pushes up for low utilization but flattens with reserved pools. Dedicated (hosted reserved) is often the sweet spot for teams with predictable load.
[06:59] Tom: security — SAML SSO and audit logs are a must, and we need per-model audit trail for compliance.
[07:07] Avery: yes, we have audit logs and RBAC. we'll include the SOC2 excerpt and an audit-log sample file.
[07:12] Priya: what's the pilot we propose? timeline and success metrics?
[07:17] Diego: propose 2-week pilot: 1) run with a dedicated 4-gpu pool on your VPC or Redwood Dedicated; 2) replay 48 hours of traffic at x1 to x3 scale, with the prefetch layer enabled at configurable widths; 3) measure p50/p95 and cost delta vs baseline. success if p95 <350ms for short queries and cost reduction >45% for top-traffic personas.
[07:42] Sofia: what do we need to provide?
[07:45] Priya: we'll provide a rolling 48-hour trace and ~2000 sample prompts, plus infra contact for KMS/HSM onboarding.
[07:54] Diego: perfect. i'll note values to tune: prefetch width (1–5), kv ttl, batch window (ms), target concurrency per replica.
[08:02] Diego: small aside — for very short prompts (<=16 tokens), sometimes batching hurts p95 because the model compute per token is tiny and kernel launch dominates. we recommend a hybrid: direct small-req fast-path on the proxy for <=16 tokens and continuous batching for others.
[08:21] Priya: is the direct fast-path available in private deployments?
[08:24] Diego: yes, it's part of the runtime. we can toggle it at route-level.
[08:28] Tom: what about quantization effects on latency? reducing precision sometimes increases throughput but may hit quality.
[08:35] Diego: right — Optimize will give quantization recommendations based on your eval prompts. in sim we model a 2–5% quality delta for aggressive quant; often acceptable for internal assistants but not for customer-facing outputs. we'll flag regressions in the eval dashboard.
[08:52] Priya: curious, what about model rollbacks/fallbacks in case a variant regresses?
[08:57] Avery: Redwood has rollout policies (canary, A/B, automatic fallback). we also integrate eval-based regression alerts tied to prompt sets — will notify on quality drift.
[09:08] Sofia: pricing ask — can you give a ballpark for a reserved 4-gpu pool for a 2-week pilot?
[09:13] Avery: ballpark in the sheet: for reserved 4xA100-equivalent it's $X/day in our sim — i'll put explicit numbers in the followup pricing draft.
[09:24] [long pause — screen share switching] 
[09:38] Diego: ok flipping to the heatmap: here's hit-miss by session length. notice sessions with stable prefixes have >70% hit after day 2. that's where prefetch pays off.
[09:53] Priya: can we limit prefetch to only authenticated users? we don't want to cache public content.
[09:58] Diego: yes — routing policy can be tied to headers; prefetch can be gated behind auth. good guardrails.
[10:05] Tom: any network topology recommendations for our VPC?
[10:09] Diego: colocate kv and inference in same AZ when possible; use ENIs that support high pps; set MTU to 9000 if you have jumbo frames. we'll share an infra checklist.
[10:20] Priya: are there licensing or IP concerns for us if we write compressed kv to cloud storage?
[10:24] Avery: we can keep all kv on your side; Redwood doesn't claim IP on your data. that will be in the legal draft.
[10:30] Sofia: slight tangent — competitors: we've looked at Vertex AI and SageCloud. what's the main diff?
[10:36] Diego: short answer — Redwood's runtime focuses on production inference economics and unified routing across hosted/dedicated/private. Vertex has deep cloud infra but less opinionated Optimize tooling; SageCloud offers managed endpoints but our continuous batching and KV handoff are tuned specifically for multi-turn interactive flows.
[10:54] Priya: ok makes sense.
[10:56] Diego: last demo slide — live sim toggles. i'll run a quick scenario: baseline vs hot-kv 65% hit. running... results: p95 295ms, cost per 1M requests $430 vs baseline $1,150. these are rough but directional.
[11:17] Priya: that delta would be a game changer. any hidden costs? e.g., read amplification?
[11:22] Diego: we include read amplification in the sim; if your avg prefetch width is high the kv ops can dominate. we model that and show tipping point in the sheet.
[11:32] Tom: operationally how do we monitor degradation in realtime?
[11:35] Diego: console has per-route latency histograms and a kv heatmap. alerts can be emitted to PagerDuty when p95 crosses threshold or hit rate drops.
[11:45] Sofia: ok let's recap next steps.
[11:48] Avery: recap: 1) Red send sim sheet + pricing + SOC2/KMS artifacts (Avery). 2) Redwood run 2-week pilot with 4-GPU config and replay (Diego to orchestrate). 3) Mistral to provide 48-hour trace and infra contacts (Priya). target follow-up 2026-10-26.
[12:06] Priya: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[12:09] Avery: thanks, we'll send notes. bye.
